schleicher_6.yay.titleHtml: Perhaps he can still be convinced?

schleicher_7.subtitleHtml: A meeting, initiated by the unions this time.
schleicher_7.bodyHtml: = The Free Unions and Schleicher Theodor Leipart and the ADGB's vice chairmen have requested a meeting with Chancellor von Schleicher to discuss the funding of Schleicher's planned public works program, which Gereke has almost finished despite Schleicher unwilling to cut through red tape to speed up the process for him. However, Schleicher has used this meeting to discuss the possibility of the ADGB endorsing his planned postponement of new elections, which the organization denounced any potential breach of the constitution. [? if prussia_leader == "Schleicher": "Anti-Schleicher sentiment has grown so much in the republican parties, that Otto Braun reversed his earlier willingness to join with the chancellor in asking the president to postpone elections unconstitutionally. ?] However, the obsession of the **SPD** and Center Party to prevent a breach of the constitution by Schleicher or Papen at all costs has caused many leaders, with the possible exception of Braun, to lose sight of the real peril: [+ nsdap_chancellor +]'s appointment to the chancellorship.

choices.labelHtml: Need not to worry, after all, Hindenburg will never appoint [+ nsdap_chancellor +]!

schleicher_8.titleHtml: Schleicher Founds a New Political Party!
schleicher_8.subtitleHtml: He seeks to capitalize on his newfound popularity.
schleicher_8.bodyHtml: = A New Political Force Schleicher, once reviled by the public, is now hailed as Germany’s savior. Through his public works campaign and ruthlessly pragmatic ideology, he has managed to win support from across the political spectrum. But a key question remains: where can these grateful voters turn to express their support for the chancellor? The reactionary right will never win over the workers, and the **SPD** is seen as unreliable when it comes to backing Schleicher’s government. In the past, Schleicher flirted with the idea of building a new "presidential party"—a direct vehicle for rallying public support behind his cabinet. Until now, he had taken no concrete steps. But with new ties to the working class and the moderate forces on the German Right, he now has an opportunity to bring such a party to life[? if next_election_time - time < 3: with the elections coming up?].

choices.labelHtml: The Deutschnationale Einheitsfront (German National Unity Front, **DNEF**) is formed!

schleicher_8.schleicher_2.bodyHtml: In terms of ideology, the party offers no clear position on the traditional political spectrum. Its program is whatever Schleicher advocates: Germany’s rearmament, a return to great power status, and economic revival through public works. The "Unity Front" portion of the name signals the party's openness to absorbing other groups, [? if kvp_formed: [? if schleicher_kvp: with the **KVP** approached as the prime candidate, especially given Schleicher's influence over the party. However, it prefers to retain a "sister party" status for now, similar to the **BVP**'s relationship with the Center. Schleicher approves, as his newly launched party has struggled to attract rural voters. ?][? if not schleicher_kvp: with the **KVP** approached as the prime candidate, given the close ties between its leaders and Schleicher. However, it seeks to maintain its independence for now. ?]?][? if not kvp_formed and dnvp_ideology == "Radical": with politically homeless former moderate **DNVP** members forming the main recruits, and Treviranus taking a leading role in organizing the merger of the minuscule **KVP** into the front. ?][? if dnvp_ideology == "Moderate": with the **DNVP** especially being courted to join, as they have supported both presidential governments in the past out of loyalty to the president. However, they refuse to offer more than continued support for the chancellor. ?] The front has also moved to recruit the moribund special-interest and bourgeois parties stranded between the liberals and the right, such as the **WP**[? if csvd_formed:,?][? if not csvd_formed: and?] **CNBLP**[? if csvd_formed:, and **CSVD**?]. [? if csvd_formed: The latter, in particular, stands out, having long advocated for a non-partisan presidential government over traditional party rule and for having a sizable political base. ?] [? if dstp_maintained: The [+ ddp_name +] and the Young German Order have officially joined the front, citing their ideological similarity with the **DNEF**. They're both nationalist, corporatist, and socially pragmatic. The Young German Order coerced the party to join despite the objections of old-line members like Dietrich and Heuss. ?] The **DNEF**, for its part, avoids calling itself a party at all, instead presenting as a mass movement open to everyone—from workers to industrial magnates—claiming to rise above partisan divides.

schleicher_9.subtitleHtml: Or the usual backroom deals and dirty tricks of politics?
schleicher_9.bodyHtml: = Election Irregularities Schleicher has made it clear he won’t establish a military dictatorship—after all, how could the Western Allies trust us if he can’t even maintain the façade of democracy? But that won’t stop him from meddling in our democratic processes, or so our informants claim. We have proof that Schleicher has funneled significant state funds to the **DNEF**. Maybe Schleicher hasn’t done anything at all, and this is just the paranoia of the anti-Schleicher factions within the **SPD** trying to sabotage our cooperation. Either way, it’s given fresh ammunition to the **SPD**'s "old guard," who now demand the party sever ties with him before we become complicit in the slow destruction of the Weimar Republic we helped build.

schleicher_9.schleicher_2.bodyHtml: We have publicly broken with Schleicher, presenting the frankly thin evidence to the public—including a shady 3-million Reichsmark donation to the **DNEF**. Schleicher dismisses it as simple politics, but many voters aren’t convinced. They’re rallying behind us as *the* democratic choice, now alert to democratic backsliding.

schleicher_adgb_choice.bodyHtml: Schleicher lacks the full leverage to force a fait accompli over the ADGB—at least for now. But we remain cornered, with few good options left. A sizable minority, perhaps even a plurality, of unionists have already fallen under his sway. And his threat is clear: the Reichswehr’s militia stands ready to act if no decision is reached before the deadline. Our good relations have kept him from forcing the issue—so far—but his patience is running out. What shall we do?

schleicher_adgb_choice_1.titleHtml: Approve the ADGB's entry into the DAF.
schleicher_adgb_choice_1.bodyHtml: The ADGB is now being absorbed into the DAF, with its new chairmen wasting no time denouncing all ties to political parties and pledging loyalty solely to the nation. Marxist doctrine is stamped out, and the radical **SPD** elements are purged without ceremony. The fall of the ADGB marks the beginning of the end. If even the workers have abandoned us—what power do we have left?

schleicher_adgb_choice_2.bodyHtml: Are you sure? We have lost our opportunity a long time ago, resistance at this point will be frivolous.

schleicher_adgb_choice_2_pro.bodyHtml: We are alone. Nonetheless, we will do everything in our power to launch a general strike and fill the street with protesters.

schleicher_adgb_influence.bodyHtml: Schleicher now wields extensive influence over the **SPD**, and even greater sway within our affiliated trade union, the ADGB. Exploiting this grip—alongside a relentless psychological campaign among the rank-and-file and open intimidation by the Reichswehr militia, which threatens action if no decision is made before the deadline—Schleicher forces their submission to the German Labor Front—soon to be integrated. The new ADGB chairmen waste no time: they denounce all ties to political parties and pledge loyalty to nothing but the nation. Marxist doctrine is stamped out, and the radical **SPD** members are purged without ceremony. The fall of the ADGB marks the beginning of the end. If even the workers no longer stand with us—what power do we really have left?

schleicher_adgb_joever.bodyHtml: With Schleicher lacking the influence to influence the ADGB chairmen personally, or having the adequate relations with us to negotiate a more peaceful solution, violence is the only option. Across the country, ADGB offices are ransacked by the far-right paramilitaries and the Reichswehr, arresting leaders, confiscating funds, and repurposing offices to be used for the DAF. The fall of the ADGB marks the beginning of the end. If even the workers have abandoned us—what power do we have left?

schleicher_cabinet_1.subtitleHtml: A Commissioner for Employment is established for planned public works...
schleicher_cabinet_1.bodyHtml: = Von Schleicher Cabinet Chancellor Schleicher has unveiled his new cabinet—retaining all but two of Papen’s ministers. His top priority, he claims, is putting people back to work. To that end, he has appointed Günther Gereke, President of the Rural Municipal Congress and a reformist economic theorist, as Reichskommissar for Employment, with a full seat in the cabinet. For now, Schleicher is enjoying a political honeymoon. The relief at Papen’s fall has been widespread, and his public disavowal of any plans to alter the constitution has calmed both the national mood and the republicans who had bitterly opposed his predecessor. The Christian trade unions and their affiliated parties have adopted a conciliatory stance, while the ADGB and **SPD** leaderships, viewing Schleicher as the lesser evil, have responded positively to his public works proposals. But the real issue isn’t popular unrest—it’s whether Schleicher can survive the no-confidence vote looming in the Reichstag later this week.

schleicher_cabinet_10.subtitleHtml: Promises of a Reichskonkordat lures them into cooperation.
schleicher_cabinet_10.bodyHtml: = The Center Party Enters Government Schleicher has concluded that he needs broader popular and parliamentary support beyond the **DSU**, and has opened talks with Ludwig Kaas to secure the backing of the Center Party. Kaas has proven far more willing to cooperate with Schleicher than he ever was with Papen, and the party itself is eager to return to government. The main obstacle, however, is the Center Party’s deep reservations about sharing a cabinet with the Nazis. To overcome this, Schleicher and the **DSU** have signaled their readiness to fast-track a Reichskonkordat with the Vatican—an offer that Kaas, a longtime advocate of such, finds difficult to refuse.

schleicher_cabinet_10_alt.subtitleHtml: Our choice doesn't matter after all.
schleicher_cabinet_10_alt.bodyHtml: = The **DSU** Enters Government With the favorable Bracht being installed at the head of the Center Party, the party no longer voice loud reservations over the inclusion of the "reasonable" **DSU** into the Schleicher cabinet, to increase its popular backing, and to tame the Nazis that can be tamed. This goes completely against Schleicher's promise to us, that he'll never let the Nazis into cabinet if we were to give him a major concession. e have been conned, big time.

schleicher_cabinet_10_alt.dsu_in_gov.bodyHtml: Wilhelm Frick is nominated to the Interior Ministry[? if old_prussia_leader == "Schleicher": —both in the Reich and in Prussia?]. Gregor Strasser takes the vice-chancellorship—a title in name only. [? if prussia_leader == "Goerdeler": Although the **DSU** would’ve preferred Strasser installed in Prussia, Goerdeler stays on—as Schleicher’s loyal puppet and as a concession to the Center Party. ?] At the Nazis’ insistence, Hjalmar Schacht is brought in as an independent to head the Economic Ministry. To compensate for the Center Party’s loss of influence, they're given an additional Ministry without Portfolio. Not that the Center can complain—not with Bracht in charge.

schleicher_cabinet_10.z_in_gov.titleHtml: Schleicher has found a new puppet in Kaas.
schleicher_cabinet_10.z_in_gov.bodyHtml: The Center Party claims its ministerial positions, with Adam Stegerwald securing the Labor Ministry, and other members taking the Transport and Justice portfolios. The Center Party also brings the **BVP** into the fold, which is granted the Postal Ministry. With Ludwig Kaas’s connections in Rome, the negotiation of a Reichskonkordat is fast-tracked and set to be ready for signing in a few weeks. However, their entry into government has strained our relations, as they had previously stood in united opposition with us.

schleicher_cabinet_11.subtitleHtml: Catholic rights across Germany are now formally guaranteed.
schleicher_cabinet_11.bodyHtml: = Reichskonkordat Signing During weeks of intense negotiations in Rome headed by Ludwig Kaas, the Reichskonkordat has officially been signed between Germany and the Roman Catholic Church. The treaty defines a formal relationship between the Church and the German state, guaranteeing freedom of worship for Catholics, and the right of the church to appoint their own clergy. Catholics in Germany are pleased, as are their representatives in the Center Party.

schleicher_cabinet_11.bracht.titleHtml: Franz Bracht is installed as the Center Party's new chairman.
schleicher_cabinet_11.bracht.bodyHtml: Undoubtedly thanks to Schleicher's meddling, Franz Bracht has been elected chairman of the Center Party. With Kaas’s endorsement and Schleicher's ability to "persuade" key party members to switch their votes, Bracht narrowly defeats Stegerwald and his more republican support base. The internal reaction has been surprisingly muted. Perhaps the Center Party’s gradual shift to the right has made a reactionary like Bracht finally acceptable—or perhaps other forces are quietly at work.

schleicher_cabinet_11.reichskonkordat.titleHtml: What will happen to the Center Party?
schleicher_cabinet_11.reichskonkordat.bodyHtml: = Center Party Conference Having achieved his lifelong goal, Kaas sees little reason to remain as leader of the Center Party—a position he had long described as a burden and expressed displeasure with. As a result, a new leadership race is set to take place within the party, with Schleicher able to influence the outcome through his connections with Kaas and the Christian Trade Unions. The candidate backed by the Christian unions and those advocating for a more interconfessional Center Party rallies around Stegerwald. Franz Bracht, Schleicher's [? if not dsu_in_gov: former ?]Interior Minister[? if prussia_coup_lose: of Prussia and the Reich?], has rejoined the party and is Schleicher’s preferred candidate. Bracht is a true believer in Schleicher's vision for a new Germany—one less entangled in parliamentarianism—and aligns with the Center's right wing, though not as far right as Papen. However, due to his lack of influence within the party and limited prior experience, having served only as Mayor of Essen for eight years, it is Schleicher's backing that remains the key to elevating him to leadership.

schleicher_cabinet_11.stegerwald.bodyHtml: Stegerwald has won the leadership vote! By rallying the republicans behind his candidacy, he has successfully blocked Bracht from seizing control of the Center Party. Backing such a right-wing conservative proved unacceptable to the Christian unions, who continue to resist Schleicher's growing influence. Although Stegerwald favors immediately opening the Center Party to Protestants, the party simply lacks the funds to establish regional branches across Protestant Germany, with recent elections having already exhausted its resources.

schleicher_cabinet_12.subtitleHtml: The Interior Ministry discovers "alarming evidence" of a planned revolution.
schleicher_cabinet_12.bodyHtml: = The **KPD** Is Banned! Wilhelm Frick of the Interior Ministry has announced an emergency measure, effectively banning the **KPD** after conveniently "uncovering" evidence of a planned revolution involving the **RFB**—including several warehouses allegedly stocked with weapons. A raid on a **Communist** party office has also produced a so-called plan to establish a new "Soviet Germany" in the aftermath of the revolt. According to the government, these plans were to be set in motion in protest against Schleicher's unconstitutional adjournment and the mass arrests of **Communist** deputies that followed. Only the state's last-minute intervention, they claim, has saved Germany from violent revolt. But Schleicher and the Nazis cannot be trusted. They could just as easily have planted the evidence to manufacture a pretext for crushing the **Communists**.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.subtitleHtml: A suspected arson attack, ostensibly by a foreign **Communist**.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.bodyHtml: = The Reichstag Burns The Reichstag has been set ablaze! The government accuses a group of foreign **Communist** agitators of arson. As the accused await trial, President Hindenburg and the cabinet insist the fire was meant to signal the start of a **Communist** revolution against Schleicher’s reactionary rule. Yet, we cannot entirely dismiss the possibility that the blaze was orchestrated by Schleicher himself to tighten his grip on power. Hindenburg, eager to endorse whatever measures are deemed necessary in the fight against Bolshevism, stands ready to sign off on sweeping actions—including a ban on the **KPD**.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight.titleHtml: Revolt! This is Schleicher's second step toward dictatorship!
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight.bodyHtml: Schleicher has no intention of relinquishing power once stability is restored—his paranoia (not entirely unfounded) tells him that the moment we return to office democratically, we’ll undo all the progress made toward rearmament, especially with Hindenburg not expected to live much longer. This, combined with his blatant constitutional breach, has finally galvanized the remaining republicans against the Chancellor. Perhaps its our time to strike?

choices.labelHtml: The **SPD** stands with the **Communists**.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight_mild.titleHtml: We'll launch peaceful protests and a general strike. Schleicher can't rule without the people's support.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight_mild.subtitleHtml: But he may seize on this as a pretext to escalate the crackdown.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight_mild.bodyHtml: We are in no position to fight a civil war against the full force of the state, but we cannot let Schleicher live without consequences. We have an array of options at our disposal, the [? if not unions_independent: ADGB?][? if unions_independent: workers?] can launch a general strike, and use the Reichsbanner as leverage, if we had maintained its strength. Cracking down on the universally hated **RFB** is one thing, but a mass republican movement? We don't know if Schleicher will budge. Our former coalition partners and members are skeptical to potentially risk the survival of the **SPD** to protest in solidarity with the **Communists**. Do we continue to bide our time?

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight_mild_2.titleHtml: The workers stopped the Kapp Putsch in 1920.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight_mild_2.subtitleHtml: And we can do it again.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.fight_mild_2.bodyHtml: We are not alone. [? if spd_alone: Well, we actually are, never mind. ?] [? if not stegerwald_path: Catholics?][? if stegerwald_path: Christians?] - [? if z_against_schleicher: In Favor?][? if not z_against_schleicher: Political Neutrality?] Left Liberals - [? if libs_against_schleicher: In Favor?][? if not libs_against_schleicher: Political Neutrality?] [? if not spd_alone: The Weimar Coalition parties are nominally against such unconstitutional acts as well. While they may not have an armed self-defense militia, they have several hundred thousand employees in blue-collar and white-collar jobs, and could completely cripple the economy if they act alongside the socialist Free Unions. ?]

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.kpd_ban.titleHtml: The "Reichstag Fire Decree" is signed by Hindenburg.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.kpd_ban.bodyHtml: Contained within the Reichstag Fire Decree are measures that nullify key civil liberties and rights guaranteed by the Weimar constitution. This grants Schleicher the full power of the state to prosecute **Communists**, radical socialists, and anyone the government deems a threat. Ernst Thälmann is arrested the following day, along with the **KPD**'s Reichstag deputies. Many others flee to Moscow; those less fortunate are thrown into forced labor camps, sentenced to grueling hours on public works. **RFB** fighters are summarily executed by special local courts. The Reichswehr and far-right militias eagerly suppress protests and replace local **Communist** mayors with [? if dnef_formed: **DNEF**?][? if not dnef_formed: Schleicher?] loyalists. [? if prussia_leader == "Goerdeler": Goerdeler, despite hopes that he would shift toward democratic rule, ignores the Center Party's objections and rules with Schleicher's full confidence. ?][? if prussia_leader == "Braun" or prussia_leader == "Stegerwald" or prussia_leader == "Luther" or prussia_leader == "Brüning": The Prussian government refuses to side with Schleicher here, and does not enforce his orders. ?] [? if sapd_formed: Alongside the **KPD**, the **SAPD** is declared complicit and its members are hunted down just the same. Are we really going to let the government throw our former comrades into prisons? ?][? if not sapd_formed: Are we really going to let the government throw our comrades into prisons? ?]

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.soviet_union_a.titleHtml: How will the Soviet Union respond?
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.soviet_union_a.subtitleHtml: The country ironically funding the Reichswehr's secret rearmament.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.soviet_union_a.bodyHtml: Despite the Soviet Union perhaps being indirectly responsible by training the officers battling their **Communist** brethren on the streets, many Soviet politicians are privately outraged as fleeing **KPD** politicians spread the news of their party's dissolution. However, despite this, Stalin has adhered to his policy of secretly aiding Germany in its rearmament through officer training and supplying armament technology. Schleicher's fears have thus subsided for now, with Stalin having near complete control over his party.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.spd_lose.bodyHtml: The general strike proves short-lived. An endless supply of unemployed strikebreakers and Schleicher's own sympathizers within the unions render it largely ineffective. Protesters are shot, civilians killed. The Reichsbanner is no match for the Reichswehr. Seizing the moment, Schleicher expands his crackdown, accusing the **SPD** of conspiring with the **Communists** to incite revolution. Germany is lost.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.spd_med.titleHtml: Schleicher attempts to negotiate with us.
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.spd_med.bodyHtml: The nationwide general strike against Schleicher's authoritarian regime has brought the country to a standstill. The chancellor could unleash the Reichswehr and far-right paramilitaries to brutally crush the protests—but for now, that remains a last resort. Instead, Schleicher has chosen to open negotiations with the opposition. Meanwhile, in defiance of the indefinite adjournment of the Reichstag, the republican parties have banded together to unofficially reconvene the chamber at a separate location, openly challenging federal authority. However, perhaps we have overestimated our strength—strikes rarely last with unemployment so high, especially with Schleicher’s sympathizers embedded within the unions themselves.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.spd_win.bodyHtml: The mass general strike has crippled the German economy, bringing the country to a complete standstill. With the Reichsbanner strong and organized, the government cannot simply crush the hundreds of thousands of socialist protesters flooding the streets. Meanwhile, in defiance of the indefinite adjournment of the Reichstag, the republican parties have banded together to unofficially reconvene the chamber at a separate location, openly challenging federal authority. The next few days will be chaotic—and decisive for Germany as a whole.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.z_break.titleHtml: The Center Party breaks with Schleicher!
schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.z_break.subtitleHtml: The house of cards is falling apart.

schleicher_cabinet_12_alt.z_break_gov.bodyHtml: = The Center Party exits cabinet With the Center Party already on the verge of breaking with Schleicher's cabinet after the unconstitutional adjournment of the chamber, this latest undemocratic act has convinced its leaders that only a united republican front can restore Germany to normalcy. Schleicher’s presidential cabinet now stands deeply delegitimized and increasingly unpopular in the eyes of the public, effectively ending his hopes of manipulating the party’s internal politics or using them to maintain even a façade of parliamentary democracy going forward.

schleicher_cabinet_12.fight.titleHtml: Revolt! This is Schleicher's second step toward dictatorship!
schleicher_cabinet_12.fight.bodyHtml: Schleicher has no intention of relinquishing power once stability is restored—his paranoia (not entirely unfounded) tells him that the moment we return to office democratically, we’ll undo all the progress made toward rearmament, especially with Hindenburg not expected to live much longer. This, combined with his blatant constitutional breach just a week ago, has finally galvanized the remaining republicans against the Chancellor. Perhaps its our time to strike?

choices.labelHtml: The **SPD** stands with the **Communists**.

schleicher_cabinet_12.fight_mild.titleHtml: We'll launch peaceful protests and a general strike. Schleicher can't rule without the people's support.
schleicher_cabinet_12.fight_mild.subtitleHtml: But he may seize on this as a pretext to escalate the crackdown.
schleicher_cabinet_12.fight_mild.bodyHtml: We are in no position to fight a civil war against the full force of the state, but we cannot let Schleicher live without consequences. We have an array of options at our disposal, the [? if not unions_independent: ADGB?][? if unions_independent: workers?] can launch a general strike, and use the Reichsbanner as leverage, if we had maintained its strength. Cracking down on the universally hated **RFB** is one thing, but a mass republican movement? We don't know if Schleicher will budge. Our former coalition partners and members are skeptical to potentially risk the survival of the **SPD** to protest in solidarity with the **Communists**. Do we continue to bide our time?

schleicher_cabinet_12.fight_mild_2.titleHtml: The workers stopped the Kapp Putsch in 1920.
schleicher_cabinet_12.fight_mild_2.subtitleHtml: And we can do it again.
schleicher_cabinet_12.fight_mild_2.bodyHtml: We are not alone. [? if spd_alone: Well, we actually are, never mind. ?] [? if not stegerwald_path: Catholics?][? if stegerwald_path: Christians?] - [? if z_against_schleicher: In Favor?][? if not z_against_schleicher: Political Neutrality?] Left Liberals - [? if libs_against_schleicher: In Favor?][? if not libs_against_schleicher: Political Neutrality?] [? if not spd_alone: The Weimar Coalition parties are nominally against such unconstitutional acts as well. While they may not have an armed self-defense militia, they have several hundred thousand employees in blue-collar and white-collar jobs, and could completely cripple the economy if they act alongside the socialist Free Unions. ?]

schleicher_cabinet_12.kpd_ban.titleHtml: President Hindenburg wastes no time signing all requested emergency powers.
schleicher_cabinet_12.kpd_ban.bodyHtml: All **Communist** Reichstag members who haven't fled to Moscow are arrested and thrown in forced labor camps, working over 14 hours a day to further public works projects, and more problematic **RFB** fighters are given the death penalty en masse, being prosecuted by special local courts. **Communist** party offices are officially closed down, with the Reichswehr's militia quickly suppressing any public demonstration or attempted armed uprising against the ban. Local mayors belonging to the **KPD** are removed by force, and replaced with [? if dnef_formed: **DNEF**?][? if not dnef_formed: Schleicher?] loyalists. [? if prussia_leader == "Strasser": Furthermore, Strasser has authorized an extensive crackdown on suspected Communist members using his authority as Minister-President of Prussia, even if said members don't pose a significant threat. ?] [? if sapd_formed: Along with the **KPD**, the **SAPD** is seen as complicit and has its members persecuted in the same fashion as the former. Are we really going to allow the government to throw our former party members and comrades into prisons? ?][? if not sapd_formed: Are we really going to allow the government to throw our comrades into prisons? ?]

schleicher_cabinet_12.soviet_union_aid.titleHtml: How will the Soviet Union respond?
schleicher_cabinet_12.soviet_union_aid.subtitleHtml: The country ironically funding the Reichswehr's secret rearmament.
schleicher_cabinet_12.soviet_union_aid.bodyHtml: Despite the Soviet Union perhaps being indirectly responsible by training the officers battling their **Communist** brethren on the streets, many Soviet politicians are privately outraged as fleeing **KPD** politicians spread the news of their party's dissolution. However, despite this, Stalin has adhered to his policy of secretly aiding Germany in its rearmament through officer training and supplying armament technology. Schleicher's fears have thus subsided for now, with Stalin having near complete control over his party.

schleicher_cabinet_12.spd_lose.bodyHtml: The general strike proves short-lived. An endless supply of unemployed strikebreakers and Schleicher's own sympathizers within the unions render it largely ineffective. Protesters are shot, civilians killed. The Reichsbanner is no match for the Reichswehr. Seizing the moment, Schleicher expands his crackdown, accusing the **SPD** of conspiring with the **Communists** to incite revolution. Germany is lost.

schleicher_cabinet_12.spd_med.titleHtml: Schleicher attempts to negotiate with us.
schleicher_cabinet_12.spd_med.bodyHtml: The nationwide general strike against Schleicher's authoritarian regime has brought the country to a standstill. The chancellor could unleash the Reichswehr and far-right paramilitaries to brutally crush the protests—but for now, that remains a last resort. Instead, Schleicher has chosen to open negotiations with the opposition. Meanwhile, in defiance of the indefinite adjournment of the Reichstag, the republican parties have banded together to unofficially reconvene the chamber at a separate location, openly challenging federal authority. However, perhaps we have overestimated our strength—strikes rarely last with unemployment so high, especially with Schleicher’s sympathizers embedded within the unions themselves.

schleicher_cabinet_12.spd_win.bodyHtml: The mass general strike has crippled the German economy, bringing the country to a complete standstill. With the Reichsbanner strong and organized, the government cannot simply crush the hundreds of thousands of socialist protesters flooding the streets. Meanwhile, in defiance of the indefinite adjournment of the Reichstag, the republican parties have banded together to unofficially reconvene the chamber at a separate location, openly challenging federal authority. The next few days will be chaotic—and decisive for Germany as a whole.

schleicher_cabinet_12.z_break.titleHtml: The Center Party breaks with Schleicher!
schleicher_cabinet_12.z_break.subtitleHtml: The house of cards is falling apart.

schleicher_cabinet_12.z_break_gov.bodyHtml: = The Center Party exits cabinet With the Center Party already on the verge of breaking with Schleicher's cabinet after the unconstitutional adjournment of the chamber, this latest undemocratic act has convinced its leaders that only a united republican front can restore Germany to normalcy. Schleicher’s presidential cabinet now stands deeply delegitimized and increasingly unpopular in the eyes of the public, effectively ending his hopes of manipulating the party’s internal politics or using them to maintain even a façade of parliamentary democracy going forward.

schleicher_cabinet_13.reichstag_reconven.titleHtml: Demand a reconvening of the Reichstag, with no dirty tricks this time.
schleicher_cabinet_13.reichstag_reconven.subtitleHtml: [? if reichstag_fire_decree_schleicher: Different building, of course.?]
schleicher_cabinet_13.reichstag_reconven.bodyHtml:
With our limited leverage, we are only able to negotiate the reconvening of the Reichstag. Schleicher has promised not to impede the chamber's right to assemble when it sees fit. The emergency restrictions on the free press and some political meetings have been lifted.
This is a disappointing outcome, but perhaps a vote of no confidence and new elections could turn the tide. After all, we will be able to harness the significant enthusiasm shown by the people in defiance of dictatorship.
The Reichstag will convene on [+ next_reichstag_month : month +] [+ next_reichstag_year +], Week [+ next_reichstag_week +].

schleicher_cabinet_13.rights.titleHtml: Demand the above, and [? if not reichstag_fire_decree_schleicher: also guarantees for democratic rights?][? if reichstag_fire_decree_schleicher: a repeal of the Reichstag Fire Decree?].
schleicher_cabinet_13.rights.bodyHtml:
With our limited leverage, we have managed to negotiate the reconvening of the Reichstag, with Schleicher promising not to obstruct the chamber's right to assemble as it sees fit. Furthermore, we secured an agreement that his government will not infringe upon the people's right to organize peacefully or on the freedom of the press, with Schleicher lifting all emergency restrictions. [? if reichstag_fire_decree_schleicher: This includes the repeal of the Reichstag Fire Decree. ?]
This is a disappointing outcome for all our efforts, but perhaps a vote of no confidence and new elections could turn the tide. After all, we can harness the significant public enthusiasm shown in defiance of dictatorship, and we need not fear further democratic backsliding—so long as Schleicher keeps his word.
The Reichstag will convene on [+ next_reichstag_month : month +] [+ next_reichstag_year +], Week [+ next_reichstag_week +].

schleicher_cabinet_13.schemes.titleHtml: Demand the above, and also guarantees for the continued independence of political organizations.
schleicher_cabinet_13.schemes.bodyHtml: With our leverage, we have negotiated the reconvening of the Reichstag, with Schleicher promising not to obstruct the chamber's right to assemble as it sees fit. Furthermore, we secured an agreement that his government will not infringe upon the people's right to organize peacefully or on the freedom of the press, with all emergency restrictions lifted. The most controversial concession was the lifting of the ban on the **KPD**[? if sapd_formed: and **SAPD**?], a major retreat and an open sign of Schleicher's defeat. Although expectedly, the **RFB** remains banned. President Hindenburg, along with the industrialists and nationalists, have now completely lost confidence in the chancellor. A vote of no confidence and new elections are expected. We can harness the significant public enthusiasm shown in defiance of dictatorship and need not fear further democratic backsliding—so long as Schleicher keeps his word. The Reichstag will convene on [+ next_reichstag_month : month +] [+ next_reichstag_year +], Week [+ next_reichstag_week +].

schleicher_cabinet_14.subtitleHtml: Certain "problematic" newspapers are taken over by the state.
schleicher_cabinet_14.bodyHtml: = Free Speech Curtailed In the aftermath of the crackdown against the **Communists**, Schleicher has since moved on to crack down on the free German press, which have been dominated by anti-Schleicher republicans, liberals, or the hated Hugenberg. The chancellor claims that the press is undermining the state and aiding the revolutionaries in its biases and fake news. We know all of this is nonsense, but Schleicher has slowly taken steps toward the Gleichschaltung (synchronization) of his regime, having recently established the "Ministry of National Guidance" in the decree in which he banned the **KPD**, to "fight against Bolshevism".

schleicher_cabinet_14.press_censorship.bodyHtml: With the powers Schleicher has handed to the new Ministry of National Guidance, fresh directives are now issued to editors, dictating what to print and what to suppress. It is censorship in all but name. Non-compliance brings swift consequences. We have already seen this unfold. The **DNEF** has been "acquiring" private newspapers and filling their offices with government loyalists, turning them into little more than state mouthpieces. Many other editors have been forced out of their posts—some for no reason other than being Jewish. [? if schleicher_spd_r >= 5: Schleicher, however, has been notably lenient with Vorwärts. Perhaps he is grateful for our past support—or perhaps he is simply waiting until we are too weak to resist. Collaboration, it seems, pays off? ?][? if schleicher_spd_influence >= 6 and schleicher_spd_r < 5: Using his growing influence over the **SPD**, Schleicher has even managed to install some of his own supporters to quietly "edit" the paper. It's jarring to see our supposed "newfound support" for rearmament—framed as a noble way to provide jobs—splashed across the front page. ?][? if schleicher_spd_influence < 6 and schleicher_spd_r < 5: It seems even our newspaper, Vorwärts, hasn't been spared from the crackdown. The offices are raided, staff arrested on dubious charges, and we can't even broadcast the truth for the workers to hear. ?] Stampfer hasn't been seen at his desk for some time now. Must be a long vacation.

schleicher_cabinet_15.subtitleHtml: The Staatsschutzamt is formed in its stead.
schleicher_cabinet_15.bodyHtml: = Prussian Police Dissolved Frick, the **DSU**, and Schleicher have been coordinating closely to smooth Germany’s transition into a more authoritarian system. The Prussian police, still riddled with republican sympathizers, remains a key obstacle—too entrenched to purge outright without crippling the force. But with the Reichswehr’s militia now patrolling the streets under Frick and Strasser’s oversight, there is no longer any need for this relic of the Weimar Republic. In its place, the Staatsschutzamt (State Security Office) has been created, staffed by [? if dsu_in_gov: Nazis and?] Schleicher loyalists.

schleicher_cabinet_15.gestapo.bodyHtml:
For now, the organization remains confined to Prussia, but its presence is felt everywhere. Local party members whisper that their phones are tapped, and troublesome politicians vanish—never to be seen again. With the police now firmly under government control, they decide which crimes to overlook and coordinate raids hand-in-hand with the Reichswehr.
Yet, their reach still depends on the willingness of people to betray their comrades by reporting them to the police.

schleicher_cabinet_16.subtitleHtml: Our so-called "revolutionary militia" is now officially outlawed nationwide.
schleicher_cabinet_16.bodyHtml: = Reichsbanner Banned Following months of state repression, the hollowed-out remnants of the Reichsbanner are officially banned. With the more moderate fighters having retired or been absorbed into the state’s militias, only die-hard socialists remain in the self-defense organization. This has given Schleicher the pretext to brand the **RFB** and the Reichsbanner as jointly conspiring toward revolutionary overthrow—and to extend the ban to both. If this ban goes through, we will be left defenseless against state oppression. Many in the party urge us to resist, while others claim that the era of paramilitaries is over and argue for preemptive disarmament to placate Schleicher.

schleicher_cabinet_16.fight.bodyHtml: Are you sure? Schleicher is only moving against the Reichsbanner because he feels confident now that it’s weak. He may be eagerly awaiting a pretext to strike at the **SPD** itself. The full force of the state is more than we can resist. You should reconsider.

choices.labelHtml: We'll go out with a bang!

schleicher_cabinet_16.rb_explode.bodyHtml: We have decided to cooperate with the government by preemptively dissolving the organization and turning over weapons before the ban is to take place. A notable amount of socialists have decided to fight on however, but without numbers or weapons, this ad-hoc group is destined for failure. Schleicher hasn't expressed the gratitude for our cooperation like we hoped. Perhaps we outlived our usefulness to him.

schleicher_cabinet_17.subtitleHtml: Paramilitaries are a thing of the past.
schleicher_cabinet_17.bodyHtml:
= Streetfighting Over
With the Reichswehr being deployed to quell political violence, streetfighting between the rivaling paramilitaries have died down in intensity, and the situation is effectively resolved.
The mechanic is disabled.

params.source: root

schleicher_cabinet_18.subtitleHtml: The chancellor only has a few months left.
schleicher_cabinet_18.bodyHtml:
= Schleicher's Health Deteriorates
Unbeknownst to the public, Schleicher has been suffering from pernicious anemia for several years. As early as 1930, his family doctor warned him that, given the stress and heavy responsibilities of his career, he likely had no more than six years to live. Now, with the added strain of the chancellorship, those who interact with him have begun to notice his steady decline into lethargy. He may only have a few months left.
In a public announcement, Schleicher announces his resignation, stating that he will soon handpick a successor to be appointed by Hindenburg. He never truly enjoyed the role, and in recent months has quietly delegated his duties to trusted allies in the Reichswehr, grooming them to take his place.
The question now: who will carry forward Schleicher's legacy?

schleicher_cabinet_18.schleicher_dead.titleHtml: Schleicher isn't the only one in bad health.
schleicher_cabinet_18.schleicher_dead.subtitleHtml: President Hindenburg will not survive the year as well.
schleicher_cabinet_18.schleicher_dead.bodyHtml:
President Hindenburg, now 86, is reportedly stricken with numerous ailments—bladder cancer, heart disease, and other suspected conditions kept from the public eye. Bedridden at his Neudeck estate, he requires constant care.
Two men of a fading generation are nearing their end.

schleicher_cabinet_19.bodyHtml:
= Schleicher's Successor
With his resignation announced last week, speculation over who will succeed the monumental leader now dominates the minds of citizens across the nation. Some believe he is prepared to pass power to a civilian, while others expect another military man to take the helm. In the end, it hardly matters—Germany has been changed forever.

schleicher_cabinet_19_alt.subtitleHtml: Hindenburg is dissatisfied with the chancellor.
schleicher_cabinet_19_alt.bodyHtml: = Schleicher Resigns! Hindenburg is beyond furious that Schleicher—head of the Reichswehr and the man who repeatedly assured the President of the army's power to crush any threat from the **Communists**—has now capitulated to our demands to lift the ban on the **KPD**. With his faith in the Reichswehr shattered, he has turned back to his old allies among the nationalists. And with the bar set so low, perhaps this is a blessing to us. Though they remain our enemies, as they were in the days of normalcy, whoever Hindenburg selects now is likely to be preferable to Schleicher’s continued hold on office.

schleicher_cabinet_19_alt.treviranus.titleHtml: Kuno von Westarp -[? if dnvp_ideology == "Radical": Former?] **DNVP**
schleicher_cabinet_19_alt.treviranus.subtitleHtml: Hindenburg's preferred choice once again, and [? if dnvp_leader != "Westarp":former?] **DNVP** party leader.
schleicher_cabinet_19_alt.treviranus.bodyHtml: Westarp, despite being once again begged by an older and increasingly sick Hindenburg, has declined the offer. Instead, he recommends the appointment of rising star and Volkskonservativ leader Gottfried Treviranus. With deep ties to German industry, the Right, and a pseudo-republican veneer, Treviranus is a candidate aimed at stabilizing Germany’s worsening crisis. Much like Papen’s dismissal in favor of Schleicher, the political class breathes yet another sigh of relief. Even within the **SPD**, many find it easier to confront the devil they know rather than face Schleicher’s dynamic and unpredictable rule. Treviranus will seek to construct a working majority via parliament.

schleicher_cabinet_19.bredow.subtitleHtml: Deputy Defense Minister. Ideology suspected to be similar to Schleicher's.
schleicher_cabinet_19.bredow.bodyHtml:
Presenting himself as a continuation of Schleicher and as another non-partisan military man, von Bredow has won his close friend Schleicher's favor. Although former chancellor Schleicher is officially retired, he still pulls many strings behind the scenes, unwilling to give up that scheming of his. 
However, von Bredow is certainly no Schleicher, he possesses no vast network of political connections throughout all walks of life, and Schleicher's personal popularity has largely failed to transfer over to his hand picked successor.
Perhaps the house of cards Schleicher has carefully built will come tumbling down?

schleicher_cabinet_19.goerdeler.subtitleHtml: Former nationalist mayor of Leipzig. Strong conservative.
schleicher_cabinet_19.goerdeler.bodyHtml: Goerdeler, an outspoken conservative on the German Right, with personal authoritarian and monarchist leanings, represents Schleicher’s signal of a return to partisan rule in essence. Despite breaking with his former party to join the **DNEF**, his appointment is seen by workers and republicans as little different from naming a **DNVP** man. Yet, the fact that he is not a military figure like Schleicher or his circle has brought some measure of relief. Though a long-time opponent of Alfred Hugenberg and his faction, Goerdeler remains a conservative at heart and is expected to continue the dismantling of the despised Weimar order. But Goerdeler is no Schleicher. He lacks the vast network of political ties that his patron carefully cultivated across German society, and Schleicher’s personal popularity has failed to pass to his chosen successor. Moreover, Goerdeler is known for his hardline fiscal conservatism and anti-social stance, having once called for the abolition of unemployment insurance during the Papen era. Perhaps the house of cards Schleicher so carefully built is already beginning to wobble.

schleicher_cabinet_2.subtitleHtml: The RLB is disappointed in Schleicher's agricultural policy.
schleicher_cabinet_2.bodyHtml: = Schleicher and the Agrarians Schleicher’s economic and agricultural ministers remain locked in a bitter struggle over tariffs—part of the broader conflict between industrialists and agrarians. Schleicher has refused to take a side, maintaining a façade of unity for the public. However, his failure to uphold a promise to continue Papen’s protectionist policies—meant to shield German farm products from cheap foreign imports—has led the increasingly right-wing National Rural League (RLB) to turn against him. President Hindenburg, like many conservative Germans of his generation, viewed agriculture as the bedrock of national life—a source of tradition and moral strength. It was he who, of his own accord, summoned the economic and agricultural ministers, along with Schleicher, to a meeting with the RLB. The cabinet temporarily mollified the situation by promising future action. Yet Hindenburg and the RLB remained dissatisfied, particularly over the government’s failure to renew a decree shielding bankrupt farmers from foreclosure. In truth, however, the RLB had long since become a political instrument of the **NSDAP**, more interested in toppling Schleicher than securing concessions. Despite the earlier agreement, they publicly attacked the chancellor—prompting an angry Schleicher to break off further talks. Hindenburg, under the influence of his *Junker* friends, voiced his disapproval. Eventually, Schleicher relented and agreed to issue a new measure protecting bankrupt farmers from foreclosure.

schleicher_cabinet_2.schleicher.subtitleHtml: Accusations of *Junker* misuse of government aid funds.
schleicher_cabinet_2.schleicher.bodyHtml: Although not directly related to recent negotiations, a scandal was revealed during a session of the Reichstag’s budget committee: a Center Party member leveled sweeping accusations of fraud against beneficiaries of the Eastern Aid program. Meant to rescue bankrupt estates, the funds were allegedly used instead for racehorses, luxury cars, and lavish holidays—at a time when millions of Germans were living in poverty. President Hindenburg himself has been implicated. His *Neudeck* estate—a gift from right-wing industrialists and the RLB in 1927—was transferred into his son Oskar’s name to avoid taxes. Though not legally contestable, the revelation that many of Hindenburg’s close friends also benefited has deeply unsettled the President, who is now inundated with complaints from his old allies. Given Schleicher’s reputation for shadowy political maneuvering, and the fact that these revelations surfaced just a day after his break with the RLB, many suspect that he orchestrated the leak as an act of revenge.

schleicher_cabinet_20.subtitleHtml: A test for the house of cards.
schleicher_cabinet_20.bodyHtml: = Discontent in the **DNEF** With Schleicher’s resignation, his wildly diverse **DNEF**—held together only by his personal authority—is beginning to splinter. Factions now vie to imprint their own version of "Schleicherism" onto the party’s platform, hoping to give the movement an identity beyond that of worshipping a soon-to-be-dead former Chancellor. On the right, there are the nationalists like Goerdeler, his Reichswehr allies, monarchists, Christian Socials, and an array of other smaller satellites. On the left, a more radical interpretation of Schleicher’s syncretism is gaining ground around the Social Patriot faction—a gathering of bizarre personalities whose ideology is best described, for lack of a better word, as schizophrenic. However, they still hold some respect for parliamentary democracy—more than many of their colleagues on the party’s right.

schleicher_cabinet_20_alt.subtitleHtml: Without Schleicher, the **DNEF** is nothing.
schleicher_cabinet_20_alt.bodyHtml: = The **DNEF** Falls Apart! With Schleicher resigning in shame, the **DNEF** no longer has a god-like figure to rally around. The factions and politicians once held together by his influence have now decided it is best to go their separate ways. The Blocparteis are freed, and the bulk of the organization — those not drawn from their ranks — has splintered off in different directions. The right-wing, more nationalist section has salvaged the party's national structures and will continue on by merging into the [? if dnvp_ideology == "Moderate": **DNVP**?][? if dnvp_ideology == "Radical": **KVP**?], now rallying behind Treviranus. The more left-leaning—and quite frankly, eccentric—elements of the movement have formed a new Old Social Democratic Party (**ASPD**), grounded in class collaboration, nationalism, and laborism. They call for a "Volksocialism", whatever that means. We cannot expect much cooperation from this group. Yet, oddly enough, the two splinter factions have found common ground—agreeing to tolerate, and even participate in, the Treviranus cabinet.

schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse.titleHtml: The house of cards comes crashing down!
schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse.subtitleHtml: The situation is far more unstable than Schleicher would ever publicly admit.
schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse.bodyHtml: The German people had only briefly united behind their so-called savior, General Kurt von Schleicher. Now, with a return to political normalcy looming, there is no place for an incoherent vehicle like the **DNEF** to rally the nation behind lofty abstractions like "non-partisanship" and the Volksgemeinschaft. With Schleicher nearing the end—both politically and personally—he is in no position to stop the unraveling of his own creation. Perhaps this will be remembered as his greatest blunder: that everything he built ends in anticlimax. Yet the Weimar system has already been gutted over the past few years. The Blocparteis will return to their independent status, and it is primarily the [? if dnvp_ideology == "Moderate": **DNVP**?][? if dnvp_ideology == "Radical": **KVP**?] that will absorb the right wing. Meanwhile, the left wing has formed a new national party—the Old Social Democratic Party (**ASPD**)—anchored in class collaboration, nationalism, and laborism. They champion something they call “Volksocialism,” whatever that’s supposed to mean.

schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse_2.subtitleHtml: The new parties do not seem very happy with the current chancellor.
schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse_2.bodyHtml: Following the collapse of the **DNEF**, a vote of no confidence is immediately filed against [+ chancellor +], which is successful.

schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse_3.titleHtml: Kuno von Westarp -[? if dnvp_ideology == "Radical": Former?] **DNVP**
schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse_3.subtitleHtml: Hindenburg's preferred choice once again, and [? if dnvp_leader != "Westarp":former?] **DNVP** party leader.
schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_collapse_3.bodyHtml: Without a clear governing majority, [+ old_chancellor +] loses the little confidence that [+ president +] had given him, which was no longer much after the collapse of the **DNEF** a few weeks ago. Westarp, despite being once again begged by an older and increasingly sick Hindenburg, has declined the offer. Instead, he recommends the appointment of rising star and Volkskonservativ leader Gottfried Treviranus. With deep ties to German industry, the Right, and a pseudo-republican veneer, Treviranus is a candidate aimed at stabilizing Germany’s worsening crisis. Much like Papen’s dismissal in favor of Schleicher, the political class breathes yet another sigh of relief. Even within the **SPD**, many find it easier to confront the devil they know rather than face Schleicher’s dynamic and unpredictable rule. Treviranus will seek to construct a working majority via parliament. The Reichstag will convene on [+ next_reichstag_month : month +] [+ next_reichstag_year +], Week [+ next_reichstag_week +].

schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_discontent.bodyHtml: The two factions within the **DNEF** have effectively undergone a split, their differences proving too vast to reconcile. With no resolution in sight, the minority faction has broken away, taking a segment of the party with them. [? if right_dnef: This unlucky minority is the **DNEF**’s right wing, which sought to transform the party into a vehicle for the restoration of the German monarchy. The ideological gulf was too great for the ailing Schleicher to bridge, leading to the formation of the DNEF-Fatherland League (**DNEF-VLB**)—perhaps an echo of the German Fatherland Party of old. ?] [? if left_dnef: This unlucky minority is the **DNEF**’s left wing, which hoped to redirect the party toward addressing social inequality and defending the welfare of the German worker. Disputes over monarchism and the role of labor in the new corporatist order proved irreconcilable for Schleicher, resulting in their secession and the founding of the DNEF-Social Bloc (**DNEF-SB**). ?] However, what is fascinating is that both factions now claim to be the “true” **DNEF**. Chancellor [+ chancellor +] has so far avoided taking sides, hoping to prevent further splintering of an already fragile alliance. Perhaps this is Schleicher’s influence at work—a political truce between two perfectly normal, merely “disagreeing” factions.

params.source: reichstag_view

schleicher_cabinet_20.dnef_live.bodyHtml: The two factions within the **DNEF** have been reconciled—by none other than Schleicher himself. Despite being weakened by illness, he has managed to pull strings behind the scenes, halting the party’s internal confrontation. For now, the ideology of "Schleicherism" has re-united the movement, and it appears that [+ chancellor +] will inherit much of the authority Schleicher once wielded.

schleicher_cabinet_21_alt.bodyHtml: = The Reichstag Reconvenes With Hindenburg making it clear that he expects a parliamentary cabinet from Treviranus, the Chancellor has moved to significantly broaden the governing coalition—reaching well to the left. The biggest surprise is the return of Brüning as Foreign Minister. Though Treviranus and his allies are interested in taming the Nazis, the **DSU** has no interest in becoming a junior partner in a partisan conservative government. Treviranus inaugurated his new cabinet within the last week, drawing ministers from the **ASPD** on the left to his own party on the right. Still, this patchwork coalition is unlikely to command a majority—and a vote of no confidence looms.

schleicher_cabinet_21_alt.reichstag_nay.titleHtml: Vote against the motion of no confidence, and tolerate the cabinet.
schleicher_cabinet_21_alt.reichstag_nay.subtitleHtml: The German parliamentary system desperately needs legitimacy. Forcing new elections now risks driving voters further into the extremes.

schleicher_cabinet_21_alt.reichstag_yay.titleHtml: Vote for the motion of no confidence, forcing new elections to be called.
schleicher_cabinet_21_alt.reichstag_yay.bodyHtml: As expected, Treviranus isn't able to conjure up a majority without the **SPD** or **DSU**. His government remains a caretaker for the time being. New Reichstag elections are scheduled for [+ next_election_month : month +] [+ next_election_year +], Week [+ next_election_week +].

schleicher_cabinet_22_alt.bodyHtml: = Constitutional Coalition Treviranus, having failed to win over the **DSU**, has now turned to us for support. We find ourselves in the role of kingmaker, while the Chancellor grows increasingly desperate to piece together a parliamentary majority—the only way to avoid being dismissed by Hindenburg for failing to deliver on the President’s central demand. But perhaps we can bypass this deadlock by targeting Hindenburg himself. With a two-thirds majority in the Reichstag, we could initiate impeachment proceedings under Article 59 or trigger a recall election under Article 43. If the recall election were to fail, the Reichstag would be dissolved for new elections. Yet the reactionary nature of the courts renders impeachment unlikely to succeed. Recall, however, remains a narrow possibility—it requires only a majority of those who vote, not of all eligible voters. Still, to make either path viable, we must secure the backing of other parties.

params.source: treviranus_menu

schleicher_cabinet_22_alt.reichstag_impe.titleHtml: Put forth a motion to remove President Hindenburg from office.
schleicher_cabinet_22_alt.reichstag_impe.subtitleHtml: A two-thirds majority in the Reichstag is required to succeed.
schleicher_cabinet_22_alt.reichstag_impe.bodyHtml: We are able to gather the support of [+ spd_r + kpd_r + sapd_r +]% of the Reichstag, with all **SPD**, **KPD**[? if sapd_formed: and **SAPD**?] deputies expected to vote in favor. [? if impeachment_ddp: The **[+ ddp_name +]** has been one of the only bourgeois parties standing up for the Weimar Republic and the constitution the party's founders drafted. We are expected to see their deputies vote with us. ?][? if not impeachment_ddp and not lvp_formed: Unfortunately, the **[+ ddp_name +]** has strayed too far from its former republican ideals, and now sees support for Hindenburg as a hard but necessary choice in the national interest. ?] [? if impeachment_dvp: The **DVP** were once staunch supporters of Hindenburg, but even the industrialists have grown tired of his antics and have lobbied the party to vote against the president. ?][? if not impeachment_dvp and not lvp_formed and dvp_exist: The **DVP** remains trapped in its reactionary spiral and will not support our motion. ?] [? if impeachment_lvp: The **LVP**, nominally a republican party, has remained faithful to its democratic convictions and will vote against President Hindenburg. ?][? if not impeachment_lvp and lvp_formed: The **LVP** has drifted far from its professed republican and democratic principles. Swayed by its reactionary right wing, it will reluctantly remain aligned with Hindenburg. ?] [? if impeachment_z: The Center Party, our ally since the Republic’s founding, stands with us to defend it. ?][? if not impeachment_z: The Center Party, our ally since the Republic’s founding, has unexpectedly sided with Hindenburg. Strained relations are to blame, as they now prioritize the survival of Treviranus’s government over principle. ?] [? if impeachment_bvp: Even the **BVP**—once deeply loyal to Hindenburg—has grown disillusioned with his anti-constitutionalist and erratic behavior, and now supports our effort. ?][? if not impeachment_bvp: The **BVP** has, as expected, remained loyal to President Hindenburg, despite their reported discontent over his anti-constitutional conduct. ?] The right-wing parties and nationalists remain Hindenburg’s most loyal supporters. Even Hugenberg recognizes the danger of a potential socialist president should Hindenburg be removed from office. The **NSDAP**[? if nvf_exist: and **NVF**?] will break with the **DSU** on the vote, and vote to impeach the president that has impeded their progress over and over again.

With a simple majority, the Reichstag has chosen to set aside our motion and instead proceed with a vote of no confidence in Treviranus first. Should the motion pass—as is likely—his government will collapse, and the Reichstag will likely be either adjourned or dissolved in the aftermath.

[+ impeachment_votes +]% of the Reichstag has voted to recall President Hindenburg! But our fight is not over yet. A popular referendum is scheduled exactly one month from now to confirm the Reichstag’s decision.
If the referendum succeeds, a new presidential election will be held to determine Hindenburg’s successor. But if it fails, the constitution mandates that the Reichstag be dissolved and fresh elections called once again.

schleicher_cabinet_22_alt.schizo.bodyHtml:
Under the influence of Franz von Papen—and apparently Schleicher as well—Hindenburg has appointed Wilhelm III, eldest son of the last German Emperor, as Chancellor, reportedly with his father’s blessing.
It is clear the chaos of the past year has taken its toll. In the end, Hindenburg now trusts no one but his dearest friend, Papen. It's unknown of the former chancellor's reasoning behind such a pick, but perhaps he would've hoped that reinstating a monarchy, the people can rally around him as they once rallied around Hindenburg. 
A bloody three-way civil war is inevitable.

schleicher_cabinet_22_alt2.bodyHtml: = Government of National Unity Treviranus, having failed to win over the **DSU**, has now turned to us for support. We find ourselves in the role of kingmaker, while the Chancellor grows increasingly desperate to secure a majority. However, Hindenburg—on his death bed—lacks the energy to intervene in the process, leading Treviranus to personally approach us with an offer. He is offering to repeal the ban on the **KPD**[? if sapd_formed: and **SAPD**?], in return for us refraining to call a vote of no confidence on his government until Hindenburg inevitably kicks the bucket. But perhaps we can bypass this deadlock by targeting Hindenburg himself. Still, to make either path viable, we must secure the backing of other parties.

schleicher_cabinet_3.subtitleHtml: With [+ nsdap_leader +] immovable, Schleicher seeks to unconstitutionally postpone elections.
schleicher_cabinet_3.bodyHtml:
= Schleicher's Backup Plan
Schleicher was never a true believer in converting his cabinet into a parliamentary one, and he undercut his own threat to call new elections by suggesting that no one would object if they were delayed beyond the constitutionally mandated 60 days. In reality, nothing could be further from the truth.
Even so, Schleicher now seeks to secure a decree—similar to the one he once offered Papen but which was never enacted, as the Reichstag president simply ignored him. Should Hindenburg refuse to issue such a decree, it won’t signal a renewed commitment to constitutional norms. Rather, it would confirm the scope of the conspiracy against Schleicher—one that now includes the President himself.

choices.labelHtml: [? if not schleicher_spd_adopted: The **SPD** will strongly oppose any effort to violate the constitution. ?][? if schleicher_spd_adopted: The nation needs a break from more polarizing elections. Let the chancellor govern. ?]

schleicher_cabinet_4.subtitleHtml: Hindenburg's loyalty is put to the test.
schleicher_cabinet_4.bodyHtml: = Emergency Decree Request Following the Camarilla’s meeting with Papen and [+ nsdap_leader +], Schleicher questions Meissner about what transpired at Ribbentrop’s estate—and finally grasps the precariousness of his position. He decides to test Hindenburg’s loyalty, arranging an appointment with the President just hours after the Camarilla’s own visit. The course Schleicher pursues is one of three options developed by his colleagues in the Defense Ministry. The first two involve unconstitutional maneuvers: either postponing elections or forcing the Reichstag into indefinite adjournment. The third option, however, is more intriguing—a constructive vote of no confidence. Legal advisors have identified a loophole in the Republic’s constitution: while a hostile Reichstag majority can pass a no-confidence vote, it cannot unite to support a new cabinet. In the event of **NSDAP** and **KPD** “cooperation,” this mechanism could paralyze governance. To remedy this, the Defense Ministry proposes a constitutional amendment requiring the Reichstag to propose a viable replacement cabinet alongside any no-confidence motion—thereby curbing purely negative obstruction. This option is favored within the Defense Ministry: it has the potential to attract republican support and avoid the civil unrest that the other two would likely provoke. Schleicher could remain in office as a caretaker indefinitely. [? if wurttemberg_vonc: A precedent has even been set in Württemberg, where the Bolz government ignored a no-confidence vote from a purely negative majority and continued to rule by decree. ?]Crucially, this approach requires nothing from Hindenburg beyond passive acquiescence.

choices.labelHtml: Schleicher's second new lease on life?
Schleicher's second new lease on life?

schleicher_cabinet_4.schleicher_2.bodyHtml:
Despite the clear advantages of the third option, Schleicher rejects it. He hints that even if the Reichstag cannot oust him directly, a hostile majority could still repeal his emergency decrees—rendering his position untenable. True to Prussian military tradition, which favors offense over defense and prizes personal courage in the face of adversity, Schleicher may find it too humiliating to swallow his pride and retreat from his earlier threats to dissolve the Reichstag.
Nevertheless, he decides to ask the President for authorization to dissolve the Reichstag and postpone new elections—despite Oskar likely having convinced his father to oppose this course weeks ago. His position is weakened by the fact that he previously brought down Papen, in front of the very cabinet members he retains today, by claiming the Reichswehr could not handle the outrage such a blatantly unconstitutional move would provoke.
Schleicher now argues that circumstances have changed. His outreach to the labor unions, he claims, has neutralized the risk of civil war, and his economic plan will soon reduce tensions. As Defense Minister, he also asserts that he has addressed the Reichswehr’s deficiencies—it is now better prepared, with greatly expanded stocks of tear gas and streetfighting gear.

schleicher_cabinet_4.schleicher_3.bodyHtml:
Schleicher requests for a decree dissolving the Reichstag, pointing out the chamber in all likelihood approve a no-confidence motion at the end in the next reconvocation. Also predicting that a new election wouldn't alter the Reichstag in his favor much, he also asks for a decree postponing the planned election. 
Hindenburg remains unresponsive. His personal estrangement from Schleicher is already far advanced, and there have been little personal contact between the two men for a majority of Schleicher's term. Schleicher advocating for the same course of action that he himself opposed when it was advocated by Papen. 
In the end, Hindenburg is only willing to provide a dissolution decree, but then he refuses to provide it to Schleicher as of right now. But to the public, Schleicher's hold on the chancellorship remains firm.

schleicher_cabinet_4.schleicher_4.bodyHtml: With Schleicher himself unsure of Hindenburg's support, and the **SPD** likely to support the third option—and potentially convince other republican parties to do the same—he now sees a new avenue out of the political deadlock. The chancellor has therefore cancelled his planned test of loyalty with Hindenburg, along with his intended resignation in the event of rejection or a no-confidence vote from the Reichstag. All that remains is Hindenburg's acquiescence.

schleicher_cabinet_5.subtitleHtml: The chancellor has all but given up attempts to stay in power.
schleicher_cabinet_5.bodyHtml:
= Schleicher Concedes
Schleicher, having willfully avoided any serious effort to preserve his chancellorship—for reasons known only to himself—has now resigned himself to the inevitable loss of a position he never truly desired.
In what is likely his final cabinet meeting, he informs his ministers that he will request a decree to dissolve the Reichstag, as a no-confidence vote is now inevitable. He fully expects his request to be denied and is prepared to submit both his and the cabinet's resignation.
In his final days, he turns his focus to opposing a Papen restoration, even going so far as to express a preference for a [+ nsdap_chancellor +] government—believing, perhaps naively, that he might retain his post as Defense Minister under such an arrangement.

choices.labelHtml: Schleicher meets with President Hindenburg, perhaps for the last time.

schleicher_cabinet_5_alt.subtitleHtml: The plan is finally completed and ready to be decreed.
schleicher_cabinet_5_alt.bodyHtml: = Schleicher Public Works Schleicher, having survived Papen's schemes for the meantime, is ready to decree a public works program formulated by Employment Commissioner Günther Gereke after weeks of work slowed down by red tape and bureaucracy. The plan provides 500 million Reichsmarks for the plan, and it's expected that more funding will arrive later if the program proves to be successful. The trade unions are ecstatic, and projected decreases in unemployment—combined with the global economic recovery, is expected to garner much public support for the Schleicher cabinet and a deradicalization of the party landscape, taking away the fuel the **NSDAP** and **KPD** thrives on. For Schleicher, the plan serves a dual purpose: to revitalize Germany’s economy in preparation for rearmament and a return to power on the world stage, and to pressure the **NSDAP** into cooperating with his cabinet before their electoral prospects decline as their base returns to work.

schleicher_cabinet_5_alt_pro.schleicher_.bodyHtml: With Schleicher delivering on a widely popular promise and the republican parties beginning to soften their stance toward the government, positive reports about him from across the political spectrum have begun to reach Hindenburg. This early victory for the Schleicher cabinet has dealt a significant blow to Papen’s schemes. The President is now more inclined to view Schleicher favorably, reducing the perceived need to bring the **NSDAP** into government.

With Schleicher fulfilling a widely popular promise, and the republican parties beginning to soften their stance on the government, it seems that Schleicher may be here to stay. While he remains vulnerable to being deposed by Hindenburg, the first victory of the Schleicher cabinet has dealt a severe blow to Papen’s schemes. schleicher_cabinet_5.schleicher_2.bodyHtml: Schleicher lays out four scenarios before the President: 1. A [+ nsdap_chancellor +] cabinet supported by the Reichstag—unlikely. 2. A presidential cabinet led by [+ nsdap_chancellor +]—even more implausible. 3. His own cabinet continuing under presidential emergency powers—his recommendation. 4. A disastrous cabinet led by Papen and Hugenberg—likely to provoke civil war. He does not request a postponement of elections this time—only a commitment from Hindenburg to dissolve the chamber upon reconvening. He is denied. Hindenburg acknowledges Schleicher’s efforts to win over the Nazis, but with that effort having failed, the President declares it time to explore “another possibility.”

schleicher_cabinet_5.schleicher_3.bodyHtml:
Schleicher returns to his waiting ministers and relays the outcome. An announcement of his resignation—prepared weeks in advance—is released to the press.
At this stage, the options have narrowed to two: a return of Papen, or the ascension of [+ nsdap_chancellor +]. Both promise disaster for Germany—and the latter, disaster for all of humanity.

schleicher_cabinet_5.schleicher_4.titleHtml: The cabinet's last order of business.
schleicher_cabinet_5.schleicher_4.bodyHtml:
After weeks of delay, Gereke finally presents his public works program to the cabinet. Though too late to save Schleicher’s tenure, it is approved by the chancellor and signed by Hindenburg without objection. The plan allocates half a billion marks to infrastructure projects across the Reich.
In the coming months, as millions of unemployed Germans return to work, it is not Schleicher, but his successor, who will reap the political rewards.

schleicher_cabinet_6.subtitleHtml: Schleicher offers his support to the Nazi leader.
schleicher_cabinet_6.bodyHtml:
= Schleicher and [+ nsdap_leader +]
In a meeting at the Defense Ministry following Schleicher's resignation, one general proposed resorting to force to prevent a Papen cabinet. Schleicher, however, strongly rejected defying the president, with his military training ruling out any such insubordination: “I am a general, Hindenburg is field marshal. I have been taught obedience.”
Nonetheless, Schleicher set up a meeting between his confidants, General Kurt von Hammerstein, and [+ nsdap_leader +], offering the military’s support on behalf of his candidacy for the chancellorship. He also inquired about whether he could stay on as Defense Minister. Keeping his options open, [+ nsdap_leader +] agreed to keep Schleicher as minister and lied about the current state of progress with negotiations.

choices.labelHtml: Schleicher remains as a caretaker chancellor for the meantime.

schleicher_cabinet_6.schleicher_2.subtitleHtml: An unfounded rumor, that Schleicher will attempt to maintain his power at all costs.
schleicher_cabinet_6.schleicher_2.bodyHtml: The day after, Schleicher sent a conservative with Nazi connections to extract more details from [+ nsdap_leader +]. Unfortunately for Schleicher, the person he sent boasted that the army command stood ready to intervene if a new cabinet didn't conform to its wishes. The Nazi leaders became fearful of a possible military putsch aimed at thwarting [+ nsdap_chancellor +]'s appointment. Talk of a putsch quickly gave rise to a rapidly spreading, but unfounded rumor that Schleicher planned to depose Hindenburg and take the presidency for himself. Through Meissner and Papen, the news reached Hindenburg, giving a sense of urgency to replace Schleicher.

schleicher_cabinet_7.bodyHtml: = Reichswehr Militia Deployed! The **SA**'s dramatic escalation of seemingly pointless violence has gripped the streets, with many innocent civilians caught in the crossfire. Their increasingly open clashes with leftist groups, driven by frustration and insubordination, have spiraled out of control. Although Schleicher admires the patriotic militarism of the **SA**, he now dismisses it as little more than Röhm's tool for a socialistic "national revolution"—a gang of thugs turning their violence against ordinary citizens. Röhm's open agitation for such a revolution has left Schleicher no choice but to ban the organization outright. But Schleicher's objective is already achieved: former "desirable" **SA** fighters have been integrated into a newly built militia attached to the Reichswehr, composed of ex-fighters and the unemployed. This force has been deployed to maintain order in the streets, working alongside the local police. However, they remain lenient toward their former comrades and display significant bias against the Reichsbanner and **RFB**. Nonetheless, this has succeeded in shifting public opinion toward the "law and order" chancellor, and further against the parliamentary system that failed to protect them.

schleicher_cabinet_7.schleicher_2.bodyHtml: It's good to maintain our own self-defense organization, just in case.

schleicher_cabinet_7.schleicher_3.titleHtml: Defund the Reichsbanner; the threat is no longer present.
schleicher_cabinet_7.schleicher_3.bodyHtml: With the Reichswehr keeping order in the streets, we have no further need for the Reichsbanner's self-defense role. Better to spend our scarce funds on electoral propaganda rather than weapons.

schleicher_cabinet_8.subtitleHtml: The Nazi ministers are carrying out their own policies.
schleicher_cabinet_8.bodyHtml: = **DSU** Policy With the Nazis in government, they seek to pursue their policy course.
